title: Nearby Places Finder: What Is Around a Point
description: Find places near a point with the Nearby Places Finder — cafes, pharmacies, stations and more from open map data, ranked by distance. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, from Times Square the everyday essentials fan out in every direction — Grand Central alone is 0.91 km northeast — and the finder ranks them by the walkable truth of distance.
quick_answer: The Nearby Places Finder lists the places around a point — cafes, pharmacies, stations, shops and services recorded in OpenStreetMap — ranked by distance. Set the point, choose the kind of place, and read what is actually near: the traveller's, mover's and scout's first question, answered from open data.
steps_intro: Name the point and the need; the map answers with its records:

body.t: A listing's claims ('steps to everything') become a ranked list with metres on it — the
Before the lease: the pharmacy, the grocery, the station, the park — counted from the door, not from the brochure's imagination.
Stranded near a station with an hour to fill: the finder is the difference between wandering and choosing.
The nearest pharmacy at midnight and the nearest clinic to a parent's new flat are the same tool at different emotional temperatures — distance-ranked, calmly.
The finder lists what the map records at that spot — a pharmacy that exists. Whether it is open at 2 a.m. is its own listing's business; the finder finds the candidates, their pages carry the hours.

Rankings run on straight-line distance from your point. The café 300 m away across a river may be a 15-minute walk — the list gives the geography; the bridge situation is the map's next layer, and routers settle it.

As current as the last volunteer's edit — usually recent, never guaranteed
popular_table.note: A place missing from the results is missing from the record, not necessarily from the street. In well-mapped cities the record is remarkably complete; the tool's honesty is in naming its source.

faq: The everyday essentials map data records well: food and drink, pharmacies, fuel, lodging, stations, shops, services and more — the form lists the categories the data supports at your point.
Results rank outward from the point until the list is usefully full — you see the nearest first and can judge the radius that matters; rural searches naturally reach farther.
A place near me is missing.
Open data is volunteer-built: a new or unmapped business may not be recorded yet. Its absence is the dataset's gap — the map itself (OpenStreetMap) accepts the correction from anyone.
No — this finder is geography, not reputation. It answers where and how far; quality judgments live with review platforms.

Results in a list I can keep?
The ranked list is yours to note or screenshot; systematic exports belong to the dataset tools, and the underlying OSM data is openly licensed with attribution.
Distance is the finder's measure; walking time is distance through the road network — the routing family converts properly when the walk matters.
Business owner — my listing is wrong.
The record is OpenStreetMap's: correcting it there fixes every tool built on it, this one included — a better fix than reporting it app by app.
